A phase-space representation of the bouncing cosmology leading to inflation followed by graceful inflation exit for
\alpha=2.76\times 10^{-33}<0
. Permission for use of this figure was kindly provided by the authors of Ref.
[
550
]
.

In the case of Type I–IV singularities described by
H(t)=\beta(t-t_{s})^{\alpha}
,
\beta\equiv(1+\alpha)f_{0}
, the reconstructed
f(T)
solution was found in Ref.
[
549
]
. A summary of the dynamical analysis for each singularity type is given below:

(i)

Type I: Existence of a stable Minkowski critical point.
f_{0}>0
leads to an eternal accelerating contraction while
f_{0}<0
leads to Big Bang
\to
inflation (with possible graceful exit)
\to
decelerated expansion;

(ii)

Type II: No finite critical points. A sudden singularity
(f_{0}>0)
or a Big Brake singularity
(f_{0}<0)
can be realized;

(iii)

Type III: Stable or semi-stable Minkowski critical point depending on the magnitude of
\alpha
.
f_{0}>0
is preferred as it generates a transition from deceleration to acceleration which can match
\Lambda
CDM
. However, the ultimate fate is Minkowski;

(iv)

Type IV: An initial unstable Minkowski singularity which evolves to a phantom
(f_{0}>0)
or non-phantom
(f_{0}<0)
cosmology.

Following Ref.
[
422
]
, use of fixing the boundary term
B=-4\Lambda e^{-1}
for some constant
\Lambda
and
e=\det{(e^{A}_{\phantom{A}\mu})}
is discussed. For
\Lambda=0
,
a(t)\propto(t-t_{i})^{\frac{1}{3}}
i.e. a Type I singularity, with associated reconstructed function
f(T)\propto(-T)^{\frac{3(1+w)}{2}}
. For
\Lambda\neq 0
,
a(t)=\left({c_{2}}^{2}\Lambda-\frac{9}{4\Lambda}c_{1}+2c_{2}\Lambda t+\Lambda t^{2}\right)^{\frac{1}{3}}
where
c_{1},c_{2}
are integration constants
35
35

35

Eq. (12) in Ref.
[
422
]
is missing a factor of
a(t)^{3}/2
on the
LHS
hence affecting the form of the scale factor.
. At
t=-c_{2}
, a bounce
(c_{1}<0)
, turnaround
(c_{1}>0)
or superbounce
(c_{1}=0)
occurs. Due to the complicated relationship between
t
and
T
, the reconstructed
f(T)
function is not derived.

Recently, a new bouncing scenario called Pseudo-Bang cosmology has been proposed in Ref.
[
1103
]
, which describes a unification of the bounce cosmology
a_{B}(t)\propto\left[\frac{3}{2}(1+w)\alpha(t-t_{B})^{2}+1\right]^{\frac{1}{3(1+w)}}
and late-time acceleration through
a(t)\propto e^{\beta(t-t_{B})}a_{B}(t)
. The introduction of the exponential term ensures the late-time acceleration for times
t\gg t_{B}
while generating a non-symmetrical evolution in the
H
-
\dot{H}
phase-space plane. The corresponding reconstructed
f(T)
function is given by

\displaystyle f(T)_{\pm}

\displaystyle=\frac{18\rho_{0}\left(\mathcal{A}e^{\theta}\text{Ei}(1,\mathcal{B}^{+})-\mathcal{A}e^{-\theta}\text{Ei}(1,\mathcal{B}^{-})+\frac{2}{9}\alpha\theta e^{-3\gamma\beta\tau_{\pm}}\right)}{\alpha\theta{a_{k}}^{3\gamma}(2+3\gamma\alpha{\tau_{\pm}}^{2})}\,,

(E.13a)

\displaystyle\mathcal{A}

\displaystyle=\gamma\beta\left(\frac{2}{3}\beta+\frac{2}{3}\alpha\tau+\alpha\gamma\beta\tau^{2}\right)\,,\quad\mathcal{B}^{\pm}=3\gamma\beta\tau\pm\theta\,,

(E.13b)

\displaystyle\tau_{\pm}

\displaystyle=\frac{\alpha\pm\sqrt{\alpha^{2}-6\alpha\gamma\beta^{2}+2\alpha\beta\gamma\sqrt{-6T}+\alpha\gamma T}}{3\gamma\alpha(\frac{1}{6}\sqrt{-6T}-\beta)}\,,

(E.13c)

where
a_{k}\equiv a(t_{i})
,
\theta=\beta\sqrt{-6\gamma/\alpha}
and the function’s signature corresponds to the positive and negative
\dot{H}
branches respectively. Through dynamical systems and observational considerations to set the free parameters, the resulting Pseudo-Bang cosmology is described
[
1103
]
.

The Universe starts at the so called Pseudo-Bang singularity described by
a(t)\to 0
,
H(t)\to\beta
as
t\to-\infty
, followed by a first inflationary epoch and a cosmological turnaround which is not of Big Brake type. A transition to an accelerated contraction of Type IV occurs followed by a bounce which avoids both ghost instability and anisotropy problems. Another phantom crossing transitioning to a quintessence regime occurs which avoids the formation of a Big Rip, leading to an inflationary phase with graceful exit without production of monopoles. Ultimately, the standard cosmology of radiation
\to
matter
\to
late-time acceleration follows which evolves towards a Pseudo-Rip state.

More recently, Ref.
[
515
]
has proposed an
f(T)
model which closely resembles the behaviour of loop quantum cosmology, and thus exhibits a bouncing solution. The work contains cosmological perturbations and shows some promising results, but more work is needed to relate it to observations.

E.4.2
f(T,B)
Gravity

In Ref.
[
267
]
, a number of bouncing cosmologies were reconstructed. Since the
f(T,B)
function cannot be solved in general, various ansatz forms were considered

(i)

\displaystyle\quad g(T)+h(B)\,,

(iv)

\displaystyle\quad-T+Bg(T)\,,

(ii)

\displaystyle\quad-T+Tg(B)\,,

(v)

\displaystyle\quad-T+\mu\left(\frac{T}{T_{0}}\right)^{\sigma}\left(\frac{B}{B_{0}}\right)^{\gamma}\,,

(iii)

\displaystyle\quad Bg(T)\,,

where
\mu,\,\sigma
and
\gamma
are constants while
T_{0}
and
B_{0}
represent the values when the scale factor is unity. Despite the similarity between models (iii) and (iv), model (iv) cannot recover
TEGR
and hence are fundamentally different. Nonetheless, the reconstructed solutions only differ by a term

\text{Model (iv)}=-T+\frac{B\ln(-T)}{6}+\text{Model (iii)}\,.

(E.14)

For the considered bouncing scenarios, most ansatz yield an analytical reconstructed solution (see Table
32
) except for most of model (v). It is remarked that the reconstructed
Tg(B)
solution for the matter bounce scenario is complex for the considered domain. Meanwhile, the lack of solutions for the Type I–IV Singularities and Little Rip cosmology scenarios is due to the relationship between
T
and
B
as it is not generally invertible.

As the solutions are mostly applicable for periods close to the bounce, the limiting behaviors have been investigated. The reconstructed Lagrangian generally take much simpler forms (see Table
33
). Starting with the symmetric bounce cosmology, the additive model yields an expanded power-series similar to Ref.
[
263
]
and similar to the quadratic limiting order behavior encountered in
f(\accentset{\circ}{R})
gravity,
f(\accentset{\circ}{R})\propto 144\alpha-72\accentset{\circ}{R}+\alpha^{-2}\accentset{\circ}{R}^{2}

[
1051
,
1104
]
.

In the case of the oscillatory bouncing scenario, two asymptotic forms are required as the evolution experiences two distinct bounces: (a) the Big Crunch/Big Bang singularity
H(t)\to\infty
, and (ii) a cosmological turnaround
H(t)\to 0
. In the latter, the higher-order contributions in the additive solution have indices
p\geq 2
which is a necessary requirement for deceleration after the turnaround
[
1105
,
431
,
1106
,
427
,
273
,
877
,
591
,
421
]
. For the former, the additive case
\mathcal{L}_{\text{grav.}}\sim T^{3(1+w)}+B^{\frac{5}{2}}
which ensures the generation of an accelerated contraction
[
408
,
412
,
411
]
.

The matter bounce scenario gives relatively simple forms including
\Lambda
CDM
and rescaled
TEGR
with a logarithmic correction. Finally, for
\alpha<-1
(Type I), the models effectively behave as
\mathcal{L}_{\text{grav.}}\sim(-T)^{-\frac{\alpha+1}{2\alpha}}\exp\left(T^{\frac{\alpha+1}{2\alpha}}\right)
and
\mathcal{L}_{\text{grav.}}\sim B(-T)^{-\frac{3\alpha+1}{2\alpha}}\exp\left(T^{\frac{\alpha+1}{2\alpha}}\right)
for models (i) and (iii) respectively. For the remaining cases, a power-law behavior arises. Here, the model (i)
g(T)
solution matches with Ref.
[
1099
]
.

The vacuum condition
f(0,0)=0
, a constraint which is used to host vacuum solutions such as Minkowski spacetime, can be explored to investigate the viability of the solution. This greatly reduces the number of suitable models (see Table
34
). For instance, only model (i) can satisfy the vacuum constraint for a symmetric bouncing cosmology. On the other hand, practically all superbounce solutions satisfy the constraint. Under the assumption that the universe is not in a vacuum state, models (i) and (ii) are both suitable choices for the oscillatory cosmology while only model (ii) works for the matter bounce. Interestingly, only the Type III singularity naturally satisfies the vacuum constraint in the presence of perfect fluids.

E.4.3
f(T,T_{G})
Gravity

A similar analysis for the bouncing cosmological scenarios considered in
f(T,B)
gravity has also been performed in the
TEGB
extension using the same functional ansatz listed in Sec.
E.4.2

[
90
]
. The reconstructed solutions generally take on a complex form which hinder their practical use (see Table
35
). Nonetheless, appropriate limiting behaviors such as those carried out in
f(T,B)
gravity could greatly reduce their form. Contrary to the
f(T,B)
gravity power-law ansatz case, except for the Type I–IV bounce scenarios, the TEGB power-law ansatz can host bouncing scenarios although in the absence of fluids. Meanwhile, the reconstructed solutions for the
Tg(T_{G})
model ansatz are only obtained in the absence of fluids, a consequence of the fact that the resulting differential equations take on complicated forms. This feature is strongly present in the Type I–IV bouncing scenarios since there is no general invertible expression between

E.4.4
Unimodular Teleparallel Gravity

The unimodular formulation has also been applied in the context of bouncing cosmologies. The Starobinsky inflation model
[
16
,
1107
,
1108
,
1109
]
can be described via the Hubble evolution
H(t)=H_{i}-\frac{M^{2}(t-t_{i})}{6}
, where
t_{i}
is the time when inflation starts,
H_{i}=H(t=t_{i})
and
M\gg 1
, and corresponds to the scale factor
a(t)\propto e^{H_{i}(t-t_{i})-\frac{1}{12}M^{2}(t-t_{i})^{2}}
. At early-times,
a(t)\approx e^{H_{i}(t-t_{i})-\frac{1}{6}M^{2}tt_{i}}
. However, the
{t_{i}}^{2}
contribution is retained in Ref.
[
250
]
,

a(t)\approx e^{H_{i}(t-t_{i})-\frac{1}{6}M^{2}tt_{i}+\frac{1}{2}M^{2}{t_{i}}^{2}}\,.

(E.15)

Transforming in terms of unimodular time coordinates,
t^{\prime}
, leads to
a(t^{\prime})\propto\left(t^{\prime}-k\right)^{\frac{1}{3}}
, for some integration constant
k
, resulting in the singular unimodular Hubble parameter
\mathcal{H}=\frac{1}{3(t^{\prime}-k)}
36
36

36

The listed result differs quite considerably from that found in Ref.
[
250
]
. While
a(t^{\prime})
differs from the one listed in Eq. (55), it agrees with Ref.
[
1109
]
even if the
{t_{i}}^{2}
contribution is included.
. Interestingly,
T
becomes constant making the Friedmann equation to become algebraic. Thus, a vast class of unimodular

Within the context of a unimodular boundary term fixing
B(t^{\prime})=-4\Lambda
sets
a(t^{\prime})=a_{B}[\beta(t^{\prime}-{t_{B}}^{\prime})^{2}+1]^{\frac{1}{6}}
, where
a_{B}\equiv a({t_{B}}^{\prime})
,
\beta=\frac{\Lambda}{{a_{B}}^{6}}
which describes a cosmological sequence which passes through Type IV bounces, an inflationary phase and a standard decelerated cosmology. Despite no pathologies arise near the bounces, the cosmology ends in a Minkowskian fate making it a non-viable scenario
[
422
]
. Here, the associated reconstructed unimodular

f(t^{\prime})=-\frac{t^{\prime}}{\sqrt{\beta{t^{\prime}}^{2}+1}}\int\frac{\lambda(t^{\prime})}{{t^{\prime}}^{2}\sqrt{\beta{t^{\prime}}^{2}+1}}\,{\rm d}t^{\prime}+\frac{2\rho_{m,B}}{\sqrt{\beta{t^{\prime}}^{2}+1}}\,_{2}F_{1}\left(-\frac{1}{2},1+\frac{w}{2},\frac{1}{2},-\beta{t^{\prime}}^{2}\right)\,,

(E.16)

where
\lambda(t^{\prime})
is the unimodular Lagrange multiplier and
\rho_{m,B}\equiv\rho_{m}({t_{B}}^{\prime})
.

E.4.5
Perspectives on bouncing cosmologies in teleparallel cosmology

The bouncing cosmological description aims to provide an alternative viewpoint to the beginning and late phases of the Universe. In the context of
TG
theories, bouncing cosmological scenarios can be generated either through a specification of the gravitational Lagrangian or via reconstruction methods. Thus, these bouncing cosmologies can be achieved without invoking any exotic matter. For instance,
f(T)
gravity can host a vast number of bouncing solutions with the possibility of realizing a suitable cosmological sequence, such as the Pseudo-Bang cosmology. Meanwhile, current observations do not lead to the formation of a Type III singularity in the case of teleparallel
DE
whereas avoidance of ghost instabilities have been verified in
f(T)
gravity models. Meanwhile,
f(T,B)
gravity can also host a diverse number of bouncing solutions which Lagrangian is able to host vacuum (such as Minkowski) solutions, and can also generate the necessary accelerating contraction prior a Big Crunch. On the other hand,
f(T,T_{G})
gravity can be used to generate bouncing cosmologies, however, only the models hosting a Type III singularity were found to be compatible with the vacuum constraint. Finally, while the unimodular formulation can host the singular bounce, the theory has not yet been investigated in detail whether it can host other bouncing cosmologies.

It is worth nothing that most of the reported analysis has been conducted within the aspect of reconstruction. An exception lies within
f(T)
gravity where the use of dynamical systems (some are also reported in Sec. 6.1.3) and its consequences in scalar and tensor power spectra (see Sec. 6.7.2) has been explored. While there has been works which briefly outline the existence of bouncing scenarios in other
TG
formulations (see Secs. 6.3.3, 6.5.3.1 and 6.6.4), there has not yet been an extensive analysis investigating the existence and suitable conditions to realise a viable cosmological bounce. More work has yet to be conducted in this sector.

E.5
Anisotropic cosmologies in teleparallel theories of gravity

In the previous sections, the Universe was assumed to be spatially homogeneous and isotropic leading to the extensive use of the
FLRW
metric. However, it is known that inhomogeneities and anisotropies do exist in the Universe, making the
FLRW
metric insufficient to describe these behaviors unless inhomogeneous and anisotropic effects are included. As discussed in Sec. 7, these can be accounted for through small, linear perturbations in the
FLRW
metric. However, the cosmological perturbation procedure also has limitations, for instance when the size of the perturbations are comparable to the background cosmology.

There are also other philosophical arguments to consider. Could the early Universe be initially anisotropic and inhomogeneous which isotropizes and homogenesizes at later times? If inflation did not occur, what other mechanism could have taken place which generated the anisotropies and inhomogeneities? Even though it has been observed that the
CMB
is statistically isotropic and Gaussian
[
1110
]
, anomalies appear at large scales including: (i) a lack of power at largest scales (quadropole contributions), (ii) hemispherical asymmetry and (iii) a preferred alignment at largest scales (quadropole and octopole). These features, which appeared in both
WMAP
[
1111
,
1112
,
1113
,
1114
,
1115
,
1116
]
and Planck data
[
1117
,
516
]
, could indicate a departure from this statistical isotropy principle. While investigations whether these are sourced from possible systematics in the experiments (
WMAP
[
1111
,
1116
]
, Planck
[
516
]
), a deviation from statistical isotropy may still be a reality.

A possible resolution is through the use of Bianchi models
[
1118
,
1119
]
, metrics which are spatially homogeneous but not necessarily isotropic. In this way, these could describe an initial anisotropic cosmology which correctly accounts for the early Universe anisotropies while it isotropizes at late-times leading to the overall observed
FLRW
cosmology. While a brief overview of the Bianchi metrics is provided, a detailed account is available in Refs.
[
1120
,
1121
,
1122
,
1123
]
.

Given a set of spatial basis vectors
e
i
obeying the relations

[\textbf{e}_{i},\textbf{e}_{j}]=C^{k}_{ij}\textbf{e}_{k}\,,

(E.17)

where
[\cdot,\cdot]
is the commutator and
C^{k}_{ij}
are structure constants, their associated dual vectors
w
k
are constructed through

{\rm d}\textbf{w}^{k}=-\frac{1}{2}C^{k}_{ij}\textbf{w}^{i}\wedge\textbf{w}^{j}\,,

(E.18)

where
\wedge
represents the exterior product. This leads to the construction of the Bianchi metric

{\rm d}s^{2}={\rm d}t^{2}-\gamma_{ij}(t)\textbf{w}^{i}\textbf{w}^{j}\,,

(E.19)

where
\gamma_{ij}
is the spatial metric. Nine distinct types of Bianchi models, referred to as Type I–IX (BT-I–BT-IX), can be constructed from the structure constants, which are further classified under two classes:

1.

Class A: BT-I, II, VI
0
, VII
0
, VIII, IX;

2.

Class B: BT-III, IV, V, VI
h
and VII
h
.

The parameter
h
is an arbitrary non-zero parameter which generates a family of isometries for Types VI and VII.

The Bianchi models have been extensively studied in the context of cosmology. In the case of the background evolution, Collins and Hawking have shown that for ordinary matter universes, most Bianchi models become anisotropic at early-times even if the Universe is very isotropic at late-times
[
1124
]
. Furthermore, Wald showed that for a positive cosmological constant, Bianchi universes become isotropic at late-times
[
1125
]
. Hu and Parker showed that for a renormalized energy-momentum tensor of a quantised matter field in a BT-I model, particle creation during times of the order of a Planck time could be strong enough to isotropize the Universe at an early-time
[
1126
]
. BT-III models have also been studied for late-time isotropy
[
1113
]
.

In the case of
CMB
anisotropies, Class B models generate a spiral-pattern and hot spot regions, while BT-IX models can affect the quadropole spectrum
[
1120
,
1127
]
. The quadropole effects can also be investigated through other Bianchi spacetimes
[
1113
,
1111
,
1115
,
1128
,
1129
,
1114
]
.

While cosmological perturbations are mainly considered for the
FLRW
cosmology, a similar approach can be considered for Bianchi metrics. As discussed in Refs.
[
1112
,
1114
]
, the approaches are distinct for non-perfect fluids and the perturbation equations become scale dependent, which introduce a coupling between the scalar and tensor modes leading to a scalar-tensor see-saw mechanism.

E.5.1
Tetrad and spin connection in anisotropic cosmologies

For every Bianchi model choice, an associated tetrad needs to be constructed such that it generates the Bianchi metric. However, as discussed in Sec. 5.12, this tetrad does not guarantee that it satisfies the field equations. Adequately, a good tetrad-spin connection pair must be considered to host a consistent set of field equations. In the following, we shall first present and discuss the diagonal tetrad with zero spin connection for the BT-I, BT-III, Kantowski-Sachs and Kasner metrics in the context of the
f(T,B)
gravity. For the BT-III case, this choice does not constitute a good tetrad-spin connection pair. Thus, we then present a novel set of good tetrad-spin connection pairs for a selection of Bianchi models which have not yet appeared in literature.

E.5.1.1
Using a diagonal tetrad - not good tetrad-spin connection pair

Based on the anisotropic cosmological models considered in teleparallel theories of gravity, only a select number of Bianchi type metrics shall be explored in detail, namely BT-I and III. Furthermore, Kantowski-Sachs
[
1130
]
and Kasner
[
1131
]
spacetimes are also discussed in
f(T)
. The BT-III metric in Cartesian coordinates is given to be

{\rm d}s^{2}={\rm d}t^{2}-a^{2}(t){\rm d}x^{2}-e^{-2\alpha x}b^{2}(t){\rm d}y^{2}-c^{2}(t){\rm d}z^{2}\,,

(E.20)

where
\alpha
is a constant parameter and
a(t)
,
b(t)
and
c(t)
are the directional scale factors. Trivially, the
FLRW
metric is obtained when
a=b=c
and
\alpha=0
. On the other hand, BT-I is obtained when
\alpha=0
while the locally rotationally symmetric BT-I and Kantowski-Sachs models are obtained when
\alpha=0
and
b=c
. Lastly, the Kasner universe is obtained when
\alpha=0
and the scale factors reduce to power-law behaviors
a(t)\propto t^{p_{1}}
,
b(t)\propto t^{p_{2}}
and
c(t)\propto t^{p_{3}}
with
p_{1,2,3}
are constants obeying the Kasner relations
\sum\limits_{i=1}^{3}p_{i}=1
, and
\sum\limits_{i=1}^{3}{p_{i}}^{2}=1
.

Next, we choose a tetrad-spin connection pair which yields the metric. One natural choice that would generalize the flat
FLRW
tetrad (6.4) is the diagonal tetrad

e^{A}_{\phantom{A}\mu}=\text{diag}\left[1,a(t),e^{-\alpha x}b(t),c(t)\right]\,,

(E.21)

and zero spin connection components, for which the torsion scalar and the boundary term become

\displaystyle T

\displaystyle=-2\left(H_{a}H_{b}+H_{a}H_{c}+H_{b}H_{c}\right)\,,

(E.22a)

\displaystyle B

\displaystyle=\frac{2\alpha^{2}}{a^{2}}-2\left[\dot{H}_{a}+\dot{H}_{b}+\dot{H}_{c}+(H_{a}+H_{b}+H_{c})^{2}\right]\,,

(E.22b)

where
H_{a}=\dot{a}/a,H_{b}=\dot{b}/b,H_{c}=\dot{c}/c
represent the directional Hubble parameters. Finally, it is convenient to define an average Hubble parameter

H\equiv\frac{1}{3}\left(H_{a}+H_{b}+H_{c}\right)\,,

(E.23)

which describes the average expansion of this universe. Consequently, an average scale factor
\tilde{a}\equiv(abc)^{1/3}
is defined. Naturally, this is related to the average Hubble parameter through the standard relation
H=\dot{\tilde{a}}/\tilde{a}
.
Interestingly, the effect of
\alpha
is absent in the torsion scalar, which has important consequences to the field equations, which is best illustrated through the context of
f(T,B)
gravity. Assuming a perfect fluid with anisotropic pressures in each spatial direction,
p_{x,y,z}
, for this choice of tetrad, the field equations of
f(T,B)
gravity result into

\displaystyle\kappa^{2}\rho

\displaystyle=-\frac{f}{2}+f_{T}\left(T+\frac{\alpha^{2}}{a^{2}}\right)+\frac{Bf_{B}}{2}+\dot{f}_{B}\left(H_{a}+H_{b}+H_{c}\right)\,,

(E.24a)

\displaystyle-\kappa^{2}p_{x}

\displaystyle=-\frac{f}{2}-f_{T}\left[(H_{b}+H_{c})^{2}+H_{a}(H_{b}+H_{c})+\dot{H}_{b}+\dot{H}_{c}\right]-\left(H_{b}+H_{c}\right)\dot{f}_{T}+\frac{Bf_{B}}{2}+\ddot{f}_{B}\,,

(E.24b)

\displaystyle-\kappa^{2}p_{y}

\displaystyle=-\frac{f}{2}-f_{T}\left[(H_{a}+H_{c})^{2}+H_{b}(H_{a}+H_{c})+\dot{H}_{a}+\dot{H}_{c}\right]-\left(H_{a}+H_{c}\right)\dot{f}_{T}+\frac{Bf_{B}}{2}+\ddot{f}_{B}\,,

(E.24c)

\displaystyle-\kappa^{2}p_{z}

\displaystyle=-\frac{f}{2}-f_{T}\left[(H_{b}+H_{a})^{2}+H_{c}(H_{b}+H_{a})+\dot{H}_{b}+\dot{H}_{a}-\frac{\alpha^{2}}{a^{2}}\right]-\left(H_{a}+H_{b}\right)\dot{f}_{T}+\frac{Bf_{B}}{2}+\ddot{f}_{B}\,,

(E.24d)

\displaystyle 0

\displaystyle=\alpha\left(H_{a}-H_{b}\right)f_{T}\,,

(E.24e)

and there is an additional equation from the antisymmetric part, namely

\frac{1}{2}\alpha(\dot{f}_{T}+\dot{f}_{B})=0\,.

(E.25)

The respective
f(T)
field equations reported in Refs.
[
1132
,
1133
]
are also recovered.

The last (antisymmetric) equation shows the problem of the choice of the tetrad not being compatible with a zero spin connection, since the only way to solve it is either
\alpha=0
(which recovers BT-I), or
f=f(-T+B)
which is just
f(\accentset{\circ}{R})
, or
\dot{T}=\dot{B}=0
. In the latter case, however, this reduces to
\Lambda
CDM
. On the other hand, BT-I, Kantowski-Sachs, locally rotationally symmetric and Kasner cosmologies do not host this issue as the antisymmetric equation Eq. (
E.25
) is naturally satisfied.

At least in the context of
f(T)
gravity, there has been an attempt to obtain a consistent set of field equations
[
1134
]
. However, it has been unsuccessful since an incompatible tetrad-spin connection pair was considered. A resolution of this issue is explored in the following part.

E.5.1.2
Using a good tetrad-spin connection pair

As we saw in the previous section, for BT-III, if one uses the diagonal tetrad in Eq. (
E.21
) in the Weitzenböck gauge, the antisymmetric field equations in
f(T)
gravity constrain the model to be
TEGR
(or to become BT-I). This is related to the choice of the tetrad-spin connection pair that is not compatible with the symmetries of the system. In this section, we will derive a good tetrad-spin connection pair for
f(T,B)
gravity for different types of Bianchi models. Let us first start with the following metric

{\rm d}s^{2}={\rm d}t^{2}-\sigma_{1}(t,x,y,z){\rm d}x^{2}-\sigma_{2}(t,x,y,z){\rm d}y^{2}-\sigma_{3}(t,x,y,z){\rm d}z^{2}\,,

(E.26)

where
\sigma_{i}
are arbitrary functions of the Cartesian coordinates. This metric is in the form of BT-I, BT-III, BT-V and BT-VI. Let us then start by assuming a zero spin connection and start with following diagonal tetrad

e^{A}_{\phantom{A}\mu}=\text{diag}(1,\sigma_{1},\sigma_{2},\sigma_{3})\,,

(E.27)

which is not a good tetrad-spin connection pair choice. Then, we can perform a Lorentz transformations
e^{\prime}{}^{A}{}_{\mu}=\Lambda^{A}{}_{B}e^{B}{}_{\mu}
with the three Euler
\alpha_{i}
angles which explicitly gives us the following rotated tetrad

\displaystyle\mathbf{e}^{\prime 0}

\displaystyle=\>

\displaystyle{\rm d}t\,,

(E.28a)

\displaystyle\mathbf{e}^{\prime 1}

\displaystyle=\>

\displaystyle\sigma_{1}\cos\alpha_{2}\cos\alpha_{3}\,{\rm d}x-\sigma_{2}(\sin\alpha_{1}\sin\alpha_{2}\cos\alpha_{3}+\cos\alpha_{1}\sin\alpha_{3})\,{\rm d}y

\displaystyle+\sigma_{3}(\sin\alpha_{1}\sin\alpha_{3}-\cos\alpha_{1}\sin\alpha_{2}\cos\alpha_{3})\,{\rm d}z\,,

(E.28b)

\displaystyle\mathbf{e}^{\prime 2}

\displaystyle=\>

\displaystyle\sigma_{1}\cos\alpha_{2}\sin\alpha_{3}\,{\rm d}x+\sigma_{2}(\cos\alpha_{1}\cos\alpha_{3}-\sin\alpha_{1}\sin\alpha_{2}\sin\alpha_{3})\,{\rm d}y

\displaystyle-\sigma_{3}(\cos\alpha_{1}\sin\alpha_{2}\sin\alpha_{3}+\sin\alpha_{1}\cos\alpha_{3})\,{\rm d}z\,,

(E.28c)

\displaystyle\mathbf{e}^{\prime 3}

\displaystyle=\>

\displaystyle\sigma_{1}\sin\alpha_{2}\,{\rm d}x+\sigma_{2}\sin\alpha_{1}\cos\alpha_{2}\,{\rm d}y+\sigma_{3}\cos\alpha_{1}\cos\alpha_{2}\,{\rm d}z\,,

(E.28d)

where
\alpha_{i}
can depend on all the coordinates
(t,x,y,z)
. If we replace this tetrad into the
f(T,B)
gravitational field equations (5.80), we get that the antisymmetric equations become

\displaystyle 0

\displaystyle=\>

\displaystyle(\dot{f}_{B}+\dot{f}_{T})\Big[\sigma_{3}\left(\sigma_{1}\left(\alpha_{2,y}\sin\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{3,y}\cos\alpha_{1}\cos\alpha_{2}\right)-\sigma_{2,x}\right)

\displaystyle+\sigma_{2}\left(\sigma_{1}\left(\alpha_{2,z}\cos\alpha_{1}-\alpha_{3,z}\sin\alpha_{1}\cos\alpha_{2}\right)-\sigma_{3,x}\right)\Big]\,,

(E.29a)

\displaystyle 0

\displaystyle=\>

\displaystyle(\dot{f}_{B}+\dot{f}_{T})\left(\sigma_{1}\left(\sigma_{2}\left(\alpha_{1,z}+\alpha_{3,z}\sin\alpha_{2}\right)-\sigma_{3,y}\right)-\sigma_{3}\left(\sigma_{2}\left(\alpha_{2,x}\sin\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{3,x}\cos\alpha_{1}\cos\alpha_{2}\right)+\sigma_{1,y}\right)\right)\,,

(E.29b)

\displaystyle 0

\displaystyle=\>

\displaystyle(\dot{f}_{B}+\dot{f}_{T})\left(\sigma_{1}\left(\sigma_{3}\left(\alpha_{1,y}+\alpha_{3,y}\sin\alpha_{2}\right)+\sigma_{2,z}\right)+\sigma_{2}\left(\sigma_{3}\left(\alpha_{2,x}\cos\alpha_{1}-\alpha_{3,x}\sin\alpha_{1}\cos\alpha_{2}\right)+\sigma_{1,z}\right)\right)\,.

(E.29c)

Here, commas denote derivatives. Clearly if
\dot{f}_{B}+\dot{f}_{T}\neq 0
(which is a theory different to
f(\accentset{\circ}{R})
gravity), the system is difficult to solve. It is also easy to see that if
\alpha_{i}=0
, one cannot have a solution for the system for
\dot{f}_{B}+\dot{f}_{T}\neq 0
. Then, we need the functions
\alpha_{i}
in order to solve the antisymmetric equations and then to find a good tetrad-spin connection pair. Since the majority of Bianchi models with a diagonal metric form only depend on the time coordinate and only one extra Cartesian coordinate, we will concentrate on three specific types of metrics:

1.

All metric functions depending on
t
and
x
:
\sigma_{1}=\sigma_{1}(t,x)
,
\sigma_{2}=\sigma_{2}(t,x)
and
\sigma_{3}=\sigma_{3}(t,x)

2.

All metric functions depending on
t
and
y
:
\sigma_{1}=\sigma_{1}(t,y)
,
\sigma_{2}=\sigma_{2}(t,y)
and
\sigma_{3}=\sigma_{3}(t,y)

3.

All metric functions depending on
t
and
z
:
\sigma_{1}=\sigma_{1}(t,z)
,
\sigma_{2}=\sigma_{2}(t,z)
and
\sigma_{3}=\sigma_{3}(t,z)

BT-I, BT-III and BT-V are subcases of 1. and BT-VI is a subcase of 3. For the three cases mentioned above, it is possible to solve the antisymmetric equations (
E.29a
)–(
E.29c
) by choosing

Case 1:

\displaystyle\quad\cos\alpha_{1}=\frac{\sigma_{2,x}\sigma_{3}+\sigma_{2}\sigma_{3,x}}{\sigma_{1}\sigma_{2}}\,,\quad\alpha_{2}=z\,,\quad\alpha_{3}=\frac{\pi}{2}\,.

(E.30a)

Case 2:

\displaystyle\quad\cos\alpha_{2}=\frac{\sigma_{1,y}\sigma_{3}+\sigma_{1}\sigma_{3,y}}{\sigma_{2}\sigma_{3}}\,,\quad\alpha_{3}=x\,,\quad\alpha_{1}=\pi\,.

(E.30b)

Case 3:

\displaystyle\quad\sin\alpha_{2}=-\frac{\sigma_{1,z}\sigma_{2}+\sigma_{1}\sigma_{2,z}}{\sigma_{1}\sigma_{3}}\,,\quad\alpha_{3}=y\,,\quad\alpha_{1}=\frac{\pi}{2}\,.

(E.30c)

Using these results, we find that a good tetrad-spin connection pair for different Bianchi models with a zero spin connection, with the following tetrads:

Bianchi Type I:

\displaystyle{\rm d}s^{2}={\rm d}t^{2}-a(t)^{2}\,{\rm d}x^{2}-b(t)^{2}\,{\rm d}y^{2}-c(t)^{2}\,{\rm d}z^{2}\,,

(E.31a)

\displaystyle e^{\prime}{}^{A}{}_{\mu}=\left(\begin{array}[]{cccc}1&0&0&0\\
0&0&0&c\\
0&a\cos z&-b\sin z&0\\
0&a\sin z&b\cos z&0\end{array}\right)\,.

Bianchi Type II:

\displaystyle{\rm d}s^{2}={\rm d}t^{2}-a(t)^{2}({\rm d}x-Kz{\rm d}y)^{2}-b(t)^{2}{\rm d}y^{2}-c(t)^{2}{\rm d}z^{2}\,,

(E.31g)

\displaystyle e^{\prime}{}^{A}{}_{\mu}=\left(\begin{array}[]{cccc}1&0&0&0\\
0&0&-b&0\\
0&a&-Kza&0\\
0&0&0&c\\
\end{array}\right)\,.

Bianchi Type III:

\displaystyle{\rm d}s^{2}={\rm d}t^{2}-a(t)^{2}\,{\rm d}x^{2}-b(t)^{2}e^{-2\alpha x}\,{\rm d}y^{2}-c(t)^{2}\,{\rm d}z^{2}\,,

(E.31m)

\displaystyle e^{\prime}{}^{A}{}_{\mu}=\left(\begin{array}[]{cccc}1&0&0&0\\
0&0&\frac{\alpha bc}{a}e^{-\alpha x}&c\sqrt{1-\frac{\alpha^{2}c^{2}}{a^{2}}}\\
0&a\cos z&-be^{-\alpha x}\sin z\sqrt{1-\frac{\alpha^{2}c^{2}}{a^{2}}}&\frac{\alpha c^{2}\sin z}{a}\\
0&a\sin z&be^{-\alpha x}\cos z\sqrt{1-\frac{\alpha^{2}c^{2}}{a^{2}}}&-\frac{\alpha c^{2}\cos z}{a}\\
\end{array}\right)\,.

Bianchi Type V:

\displaystyle{\rm d}s^{2}={\rm d}t^{2}-a(t)^{2}\,{\rm d}x^{2}-e^{-2mx}\Big(b(t)^{2}\,{\rm d}y^{2}+c(t)^{2}\,{\rm d}z^{2}\Big)\,,

(E.31s)

\displaystyle e^{\prime}{}^{A}{}_{\mu}=\left(\begin{array}[]{cccc}1&0&0&0\\
0&0&\frac{2mbc}{a}e^{-2mx}&ce^{-mx}\sqrt{1-\frac{4m^{2}c^{2}e^{-2mx}}{a^{2}}}\\
0&a\cos z&-be^{-mx}\sin z\sqrt{1-\frac{4m^{2}c^{2}e^{-2mx}}{a^{2}}}&\frac{2mc^{2}e^{-2mx}\sin z}{a}\\
0&a\sin z&be^{-mx}\cos z\sqrt{1-\frac{4m^{2}c^{2}e^{-2mx}}{a^{2}}}&-\frac{2mc^{2}e^{-2mx}\cos z}{a}\\
\end{array}\right).

Bianchi Type VI:

\displaystyle{\rm d}s^{2}={\rm d}t^{2}-a(t)^{2}e^{-2mz}\,{\rm d}x^{2}-b(t)^{2}e^{2nz}\,{\rm d}y^{2}-c(t)^{2}\,{\rm d}z^{2}\,,

(E.31z)

\displaystyle e^{\prime}{}^{A}{}_{\mu}=\left(\begin{array}[]{cccc}1&0&0&0\\
0&ae^{-mz}\cos y\sqrt{\frac{c^{2}-b^{2}(m-n)^{2}e^{2nz}}{c^{2}}}&\frac{b^{2}(n-m)e^{2nz}\cos y}{c}&c\sin y\\
0&ae^{-mz}\sin y\sqrt{\frac{c^{2}-b^{2}(m-n)^{2}e^{2nz}}{c^{2}}}&\frac{b^{2}(n-m)e^{2nz}\sin y}{c}&-c\cos y\\
0&\frac{ab(m-n)e^{z(n-m)}}{c}&be^{nz}\sqrt{\frac{c^{2}-b^{2}(m-n)^{2}e^{2nz}}{c^{2}}}&0\\
\end{array}\right)\,.

Bianchi Type IX:

\displaystyle{\rm d}s^{2}={\rm d}t^{2}-a(t)^{2}({\rm d}x-\cos y\,{\rm d}z)^{2}-b(t)^{2}\left({\rm d}y^{2}+\sin^{2}y\,{\rm d}z^{2}\right)\,,

(E.31ag)

\displaystyle e^{\prime}{}^{A}{}_{\mu}=\left(\begin{array}[]{cccc}1&0&0&0\\
0&0&-b\cos x&b\sin x\sin y\\
0&a&0&-a\cos y\\
0&0&b\sin x&b\cos x\sin y\\
\end{array}\right)\,.

Here, we have also used the same idea for other Bianchi models having cross terms in the metric. All of these tetrads are new results that have not been reported in the literature. It is also possible to make a Lorentz transformation to switch on the spin connection and rewrite the above tetrads in another way. It is important to mention that these good tetrad-spin connection pairs were found in
f(T,B)
gravity but, it can be shown that they are also good pairs for other more general modified teleparallel theories such as those with scalar fields
f(T,B,\phi,X)
with
\phi=\phi(t)
.

Let us now re-derive the equations for the BT-III with the correct good tetrad-spin connection given by Eq. (
E.31
) with a zero spin connection. For this spacetime the torsion scalar and the boundary term becomes

\displaystyle T

\displaystyle=-\frac{2\alpha^{2}}{a^{2}}-2(H_{a}H_{b}+H_{a}H_{c}+H_{b}H_{c})\,,

(E.32a)

\displaystyle B

\displaystyle=-2\left[\dot{H}_{a}+\dot{H}_{b}+\dot{H}_{c}+(H_{a}+H_{b}+H_{c})^{2}\right]\,,

(E.32b)

where we clearly see that
\alpha
now appears in
T
and does not appear in
B
. The cosmological equations then yield

\displaystyle\kappa^{2}\rho

\displaystyle=-\frac{f}{2}+f_{T}\left(T+\frac{\alpha^{2}}{a^{2}}\right)+\frac{Bf_{B}}{2}+\dot{f}_{B}\left(H_{a}+H_{b}+H_{c}\right)\,,

(E.33a)

\displaystyle-\kappa^{2}p_{x}

\displaystyle=-\frac{f}{2}-f_{T}\left[\frac{\alpha^{2}}{a^{2}}+(H_{b}+H_{c})^{2}+H_{a}(H_{b}+H_{c})+\dot{H}_{b}+\dot{H}_{c}\right]-\left(H_{b}+H_{c}\right)\dot{f}_{T}+\frac{Bf_{B}}{2}+\ddot{f}_{B}\,,

(E.33b)

\displaystyle-\kappa^{2}p_{y}

\displaystyle=-\frac{f}{2}-f_{T}\left[\frac{\alpha^{2}}{a^{2}}+(H_{a}+H_{c})^{2}+H_{b}(H_{a}+H_{c})+\dot{H}_{a}+\dot{H}_{c}\right]-\left(H_{a}+H_{c}\right)\dot{f}_{T}+\frac{Bf_{B}}{2}+\ddot{f}_{B}\,,

(E.33c)

\displaystyle-\kappa^{2}p_{z}

\displaystyle=-\frac{f}{2}-f_{T}\left[(H_{b}+H_{a})^{2}+H_{c}(H_{b}+H_{a})+\dot{H}_{b}+\dot{H}_{a}\right]-\left(H_{a}+H_{b}\right)\dot{f}_{T}+\frac{Bf_{B}}{2}+\ddot{f}_{B}\,,

(E.33d)

\displaystyle 0

\displaystyle=\alpha\left(H_{a}-H_{b}\right)f_{T}\,.

(E.33e)

We can notice a big difference between these field equations and the ones derived using the incorrect tetrad (
E.24a
)–(
E.24e
), which is that one does not have the antisymmetric equation (
E.25
). This equation is the one which constrains the model to be
\alpha=0
or
f_{TT}=0
(
GR
) or
\dot{T}=0
(
GR
again). Exactly as in
GR
(and
TEGR
), from Eq. (
E.33e
) one notices that one needs a fluid having a linear momentum with components
T_{01}=T_{10}
in order to construct a BT-III with
H_{a}\neq H_{b}
(or equivalently
a\neq b
). One interesting feature here is that for
f=F(B)
gravity (without having
GR
in the background), one can study BT-III with
a\neq b
for an anisotropic fluid without requiring to have a fluid with linear momentum. This feature cannot be achieved in
GR
.

This explicit example related to BT-III shows that it is very important to be careful choosing the correct tetrad-spin connection pair when one is studying certain non-trivial geometries. It is important to mention that the vast majority of the literature related to anisotropic cosmology in
TG
did not consider this important point, and for this, many of them give incorrect conclusions about these models. As a future work, it would be interesting to re-analyze different Bianchi models using the correct tetrads shown here.

E.5.2
Reconstruction method

Reconstructing the gravitational Lagrangian in anisotropic universes has been vastly investigated in curvature-based theories
[
1135
,
1136
,
1137
,
1138
]
. In contrast to the
FLRW
case, the reconstruction approach is not straightforward due to an anisotropic metric and matter fluid, requiring further considerations and assumptions prior to solving for the unknown gravitational Lagrangian. Even if a cosmological evolution is assumed, one then has to consider whether this behavior is observed in particular directions or as an average expansion which may lead to distinguishable directional expansions. In what follows, various known cosmologies shall be examined in detail.

E.5.2.1
de Sitter Spacetime

In the first scenario, each individual direction is assumed to evolve following a de Sitter expansion behavior. However, each direction may not necessarily be expanding at the same rate, otherwise it reduces to the
FLRW
cosmology. This approach has been considered in Refs.
[
1132
,
1139
,
1140
]
using BT-I where the directional scale factors are taken to be in the form

a(t)\propto e^{H_{a,0}t}\,,\quad b(t)\propto e^{H_{b,0}t}\,,\quad c(t)\propto e^{H_{c,0}t}\,,

(E.34)

where
H_{a,b,c,0}
are constants. Note that the torsion scalar is now constant,
T_{0}
. Assuming an isotropic fluid with constant
EoS
, the following scenarios are obtained:

1.

w=-1
: The fluid behaves as a cosmological constant leading to the condition

\kappa^{2}\rho=-\frac{f(T_{0})}{2}+T_{0}f_{T}(T_{0})\,,

(E.35)

where
\rho
is now constant in time. Choosing an
f(T)
function leads to an algebraic relation between
H_{a,b,c,0}
which, however, constrains the geometry to reduce to the
FLRW
one. Alternatively, treating the equation as an ordinary differential equation gives the class of functions which naturally host the de Sitter behavior. The latter has been considered in Refs.
[
1139
,
1140
]
where the matter fluid is assumed to behave as
HDE
, for which the
f(T)
Lagrangian reduces to a
TEGR
rescaling.

2.

H_{a,0}+H_{b,0}+H_{c,0}=0
: This implies that a decelerated expansion occurs along at least one spatial direction.

The second scenario focuses on when the average Hubble parameter is a constant,
H_{0}
. As investigated in Ref.
[
1141
]
for the locally rotationally symmetric BT-I cosmology
(b=c)
, this assumption imposes the condition
ab^{2}\propto e^{3H_{0}t}
which is insufficient to reconstruct the Lagrangian. To this end, the anisotropic fluid is parametrized to behave as a cosmological constant at late-times through

p_{x}=w_{x}\rho\,,\quad p_{y}=p_{z}=(w_{x}+\delta)\rho\,,

(E.36)

where
\delta
is the skewness parameter and
w_{x}
is chosen to be
-1
. In the special case of
TEGR
, an analytical form for the directional scale factors are obtained,

a(t)\propto e^{H_{0}t}\left(\frac{\gamma}{H_{0}}+3\lambda e^{-3H_{0}t}\right)^{-\frac{2}{3}}\,,\quad b(t)=e^{H_{0}t}\left(\frac{\gamma}{H_{0}}+3\lambda e^{-3H_{0}t}\right)^{\frac{1}{3}}\,,

(E.37)

where
\gamma,\lambda
are integration constants. Consequently, the skewness parameter takes on the following form

\delta=-\frac{27{H_{0}}^{2}\lambda^{2}e^{-3H_{0}t}}{\gamma\left(\gamma e^{3H_{0}t}+6H_{0}\lambda\right)}\,.

(E.38)

Evidently, this becomes a realistic model for a de Sitter late-time cosmology since, at late-times,
A\simeq B
and
\delta\to 0
, meaning this Universe becomes isotropized.

From these considerations, the reconstruction method is then applied to obtain a functional form of the
f(T)
Lagrangian with the assumption that the directional scale factors take on the previously obtained forms Eq. (
E.37
). Careful re-examination of the work reveals that the continuity equation does not lead to the ordinary differential equation
1+f_{T}-f_{TT}=0
as reported in Ref.
[
1141
]
, but reduces to an identity relation. In other words, the continuity equation is insufficient to constrain the Lagrangian. Further considerations of the fluid behavior, either through
w_{x}
or
\delta
, may be sufficient to reconstruct the
f(T)
function.

E.5.2.2
Power-law behavior

Throughout the works in Refs.
[
1132
,
1142
,
1139
,
1140
,
1143
]
, a power-law behavior has been considered for reconstruction. First, the standard power-law behavior

a(t)\propto t^{p_{1}}\,,\quad b(t)\propto t^{p_{2}}\,,\quad c(t)\propto t^{p_{3}}\,,

(E.39)

where
p_{1,2,3}
are constants, is considered. This simple ansatz can host the Kasner metric provided that
p_{1,2,3}
obey the Kasner relations. However, the introduction of an arbitrary
f(T)
Lagrangian has important consequences to the existence of the Kasner metric or the form of the Kasner relations. Similar considerations appear in other modified theories of gravity
[
1144
,
1145
,
1146
,
1147
]
. To illustrate this, starting from the torsion scalar, which is given to be

T=-2t^{-2}\left(p_{1}p_{2}+p_{1}p_{3}+p_{2}p_{3}\right)\,,

(E.40)

is zero for a standard Kasner universe. In the absence of matter fluids, the Kasner cosmology is a solution to the field equations if
f(0)=0
provided that
|f_{T}(0)|
,
|f_{TT}(0)|<\infty
37
37

37

A more general consideration can be taken, for example
|f_{T}(0)|\to\infty
but
|Tf_{T}|_{T\to 0}<\infty
but this has not been investigated in detail.
. This allows for an extensive class of functions which can host the Kasner cosmology, including (i) power-law
f(T)\propto(-T)^{n}
for
n>0
, and (ii) exponential
f(T)=-T-Te^{-pT}
,
p
is some constant
[
1142
,
1148
]
.

Alternatively, a Kasner metric is obtained through the modification of Kasner’s relations
[
1142
]
. For instance, in the absence of matter fluids and taking
f(T)\propto(-T)^{n}
for
n>0
, the field equations are satisfied if
T=0
, which lead to the following modified Kasner relations:

\displaystyle n>0:

\displaystyle\sum\limits_{i=1}^{3}p_{i}=2n-1\,,

\displaystyle\sum\limits_{i=1}^{3}{p_{i}}^{2}=(2n-1)^{2}\,,

(E.41a)

\displaystyle n>1:

\displaystyle\sum\limits_{i=1}^{3}p_{i}=C_{0}\,,

\displaystyle\sum\limits_{i=1}^{3}{p_{i}}^{2}={C_{0}}^{2}\,,

(E.41b)

where
C_{0}
is some arbitrary constant. It can be observed that the standard Kasner universe is recovered only for
n\geq 1
by setting
C_{0}=1
, while a non-standard one is obtained for
0<n<1
.

For non-Kasner cosmologies, a perfect isotropic fluid was considered in Refs.
[
1132
,
1139
,
1140
,
1143
]
including constant
EoS
w
, Ricci Dark Energy (RDE), New Agegraphic Dark Energy (NADE) and
HDE
(including their PLE corrections) fluid types. For the constant
EoS
case, the reconstructed Lagrangian is

f(T)=\frac{2\kappa^{2}\rho_{0}}{-1+(1+w)(p_{1}+p_{2}+p_{3})}\left(\frac{-T}{2\chi}\right)^{n},\quad\chi\equiv p_{1}p_{2}+p_{1}p_{3}+p_{2}p_{3}\neq 0\,.

(E.42)

Here, an expanding universe is obtained when
\chi<0
which imposes the extra necessary condition
(1+w)\beta=2n
,
n\in\mathbb{N}
, in order to maintain a real Lagrangian. Furthermore, the field equations give rise to two possible scenarios
[
1132
]
:

1.

w(p_{1}+p_{2}+p_{3})=1
: Yields an anisotropic expansion within an isotropic fluid;

2.

p_{1}=p_{2}=p_{3}
: Reduces to
FLRW
cosmology.

For the remaining fluids, the reconstruction procedure was applied within an locally rotationally symmetric BT-I cosmology where the scale factors take on either standard power-law or pole-like forms satisfying
38
38

38

The index
h
as seen in Refs.
[
1139
,
1140
]
has been redefined in order to simplify the results. The original solutions are recovered via the transformation
h\to-h
. In the case of Ref.
[
1143
]
, the transformations
h\to-mh
and
m\to 1/m
need to be applied.

a(t)=b(t)^{\frac{1}{m}},\text{ with }b(t)=b_{0}(t_{s}-t)^{mh}\,,

(E.43)

where
b_{0},m,h
are constants and
t_{s}\geq t
represents the time of a future singularity. For these cases, the
f(T)
Lagrangian was reconstructed and are summarized in Table
37
. It is remarked that in Ref.
[
1139
]
, the correct reconstructed solution is the pole-like one but the solution remains identical for the non-pole-like case. Furthermore, the solutions for PLECHDE and PLECNADE as given in Ref.
[
1143
]
are based on assuming the future event horizon and the conformal time computed based on the expansion of
b(t)
as opposed to the average scale factor. Overall, it is observed that the models reduce to power-law type models.

. Here,

for the PLE corrections of both

.

E.5.2.3
\Lambda
CDM behavior

The
\Lambda
CDM
cosmology has been studied in Refs.
[
1149
,
1150
]
for a perfect isotropic matter fluid with constant
EoS
w
. Here, the cosmology is built on the principle that the average expansion is
\Lambda
CDM
, meaning it obeys the same evolution equation
H^{2}={H_{0}}^{2}\left(\Omega_{\rm m0}\tilde{a}^{-3}+\Omega_{\Lambda}\right)
. However, since
\tilde{a}
and
H
are now the average quantities, each spatial direction may now evolve differently from one another without each individually exhibiting a behavior similar to the
\Lambda
CDM
cosmology.

To reconstruct the Lagrangian, the matter fluid is expressed in terms of the torsion scalar as

\rho=\rho_{0}\left(\frac{J-T-9{H_{0}}^{2}\Omega_{\Lambda}}{9{H_{0}}^{2}\Omega_{\rm m0}}\right)^{1+w}\,,

(E.44)

where
\rho_{0}
is some constant and
J\coloneqq{H_{a}}^{2}+{H_{b}}^{2}+{H_{c}}^{2}
. Then, using the Friedmann equations lead to the solution

f(T)=\sqrt{-T}\int\limits^{-T}_{0}\frac{\kappa^{2}\rho_{0}}{x^{3/2}}\left(\frac{J-x-9{H_{0}}^{2}\Omega_{\Lambda}}{9{H_{0}}^{2}\Omega_{\rm m0}}\right)^{1+w}\;{\rm d}x\,.

(E.45)

Here, the solution has been generalized for an arbitrary
EoS
. It is remarked that the signature of the
f_{T}
coefficient of the Friedmann equation in Refs.
[
1149
,
1150
]
is incorrect while the
\sin\theta
contributions in Ref.
[
1150
]
should not appear. Evidently, contrary to the
FLRW
case, an analytical expression cannot be obtained because
J
cannot be solely expressed in terms of
T
. Nonetheless, prior knowledge of the directional scale factors would resolve this issue.

E.5.2.4
Unification of matter and dark energy behaviors

The reconstruction for a unification of matter and
DE
domination epochs has been explored in Ref.
[
1132
]
. In particular, the model follows a similar approach to the one encountered in Ref.
[
457
]
but is now applied to the anisotropic BT-I cosmology. Here, each directional scale factor evolves as
e^{h_{i}(t)\ln t}
where each
h_{i}(t)
is a slowly varying function chosen to be

h_{i}(t)=\frac{h_{i,1}+h_{i,2}\zeta t^{2}}{1+\zeta t^{2}}\,,

(E.46)

where
h_{i,1},h_{i,2}
and
\zeta
are positive constants. This choice signifies a directional decelerating era for
0<h_{i}<1
and an accelerating era for
h_{i}>1
. Contrary to the
FLRW
case, however, the average expansion behavior of this universe may be different. This can be observed from the deceleration parameter

q\sim-1+\frac{3}{h_{x}+h_{y}+h_{z}}\equiv-1+\frac{1}{\tilde{h}}\,,

(E.47)

with
\tilde{h}
representing the average of the slowly varying parameters. On average, deceleration is obtained when
0<\tilde{h}<1
while acceleration for
\bar{h}>1
, which implies that at least one spatial direction could have an opposite expansion behavior from the average one.

Due to the complexity of the resulting field equations, an isotropic fluid as well a Kantowski-Sachs metric is assumed. As
h_{i}
are slowly varying
(\dot{h}_{i}\sim\ddot{h}_{i}\sim 0)
, the reconstructed Lagrangian takes on the form
39
39

39

The solution obtained in Ref.
[
1132
]
is not recovered.

f(T)\propto\exp\left\{-\frac{1}{2}(1+w)\left[\ln\left(1+\zeta\Psi_{0}(T)\right)(h_{x,2}+2h_{y,2})+(h_{x,1}+2h_{y,1})\ln\left(\frac{\Psi_{0}(T)}{1+\zeta\Psi_{0}(T)}\right)\right]\right\}\,,

(E.48)

where
\Psi_{0}(T)
is the real root to the polynomial

\displaystyle 0

\displaystyle=\zeta^{2}T{\Psi_{0}}^{3}+(2\zeta T+2\zeta^{2}X){\Psi_{0}}^{2}+(T+2\zeta Z)\Psi_{0}+2Y\,,

(E.49a)

\displaystyle X

\displaystyle\equiv h_{x,2}h_{y,2}+h_{x,2}h_{z,2}+h_{y,2}h_{z,2},\hskip 5.69054ptY\equiv h_{x,1}h_{y,1}+h_{x,1}h_{z,1}+h_{y,1}h_{z,1}\,,

(E.49b)

\displaystyle Z

\displaystyle\equiv h_{x,1}h_{y,2}+h_{x,2}h_{y,1}+h_{x,1}h_{z,2}+h_{x,2}h_{z,1}+h_{y,1}h_{z,2}+h_{y,2}h_{z,1}\,.

(E.49c)

During early- and late-times, the Lagrangian takes on a more simplified form:

At early-times:

\displaystyle\hskip-56.9055ptf(T)\propto\Psi_{0}(T)^{-\frac{1+w}{2}(h_{x,1}+2h_{y,1})}\,,

(E.50a)

At late-times:

\displaystyle\hskip-56.9055ptf(T)\propto\Psi_{0}(T)^{-\frac{1+w}{2}(h_{x,2}+2h_{y,2})}\,.

(E.50b)

Observe that at early-times, the reconstructed form depends on the constants
h_{i,1}
which highlight the early-time dominant behavior as seen from Eq. (
E.46
). Likewise, the late-time reconstructed form is dependent on
h_{i,2}
as expected.

E.5.3
Noether’s symmetry approach

The application of Noether symmetry for anisotropic cosmologies has been explored in curvature-based theories. Searching for the existence of such symmetries allow for the simplification of the field equations while exploring the nature of the anisotropic cosmology, for instance, whether the latter isotropizes at late-times. Some works include, but are not limited to, Refs.
[
1151
,
468
,
1152
,
1153
,
1154
,
1155
]
. In the context of
TG
, Refs.
[
1156
,
1157
,
1158
]
are reviewed.

Starting with
f(T)
gravity, Ref.
[
1157
]
considers a Kantowski-Sachs spacetime in polar coordinates. However, the chosen diagonal tetrad
{e^{A}}_{\mu}=\text{diag}\left(1,a,b,b\sin\theta\right)
proves to be problematic as the spin connection becomes non-zero which is not considered in the work. This is due the fact that the antisymmetric field equations were not checked for consistency. Thus, the resulting Noether symmetries and cosmologies may not be entirely correct.

In Ref.
[
1156
]
, a BT-I metric was considered with a configuration space
\mathbb{Q}=\{t,a,b,c,T\}
. The Noether constraint imposes the functional Lagrangian to
f(T)=-T+mT^{n}
for some constants
m
and
n
which, depending on the magnitude of
n
(
n=1
or
n\neq 1
), different Noether symmetries are obtained. However, it is remarked that Eq. (22) in Ref.
[
1156
]
is missing a factor of
T
for the
f_{TT}
coefficients which may introduce more symmetries than those reported. While the resulting cosmology was not analyzed for
n\neq 1
, the directional scale factors have been solved for
n=1
(i.e.
TEGR
) when the matter fluid is absent. However, the scale factors do not host a simple analytic form and hence were not analyzed in detail.

Besides, the anisotropic scenario, Ref.
[
1156
]
explores the
FLRW
limit where only a number of Noether symmetries remain. However, these do not match those investigated in Sec. 6.1.2 due to how the configuration space and the Noether condition are treated. When the
FLRW
limit is considered, the configuration space dimension
\mathbb{Q}
decreases, adequately reducing the number of partial differential equations arising from the Noether condition. Thus, in order to correctly recover the system of equations, the
FLRW
limit must be taken before the Noether condition is considered. In fact, the partial differential equation
[
1156
]

c\,\eta_{1,a}+b\,\eta_{4,a}=0\,,

(E.51)

introduces the constraint
\tilde{a}\,\eta_{1,\tilde{a}}=0
, where
\tilde{a}
now becomes the standard isotropic
FLRW
scale factor since
a=b=c=\tilde{a}
. This extra constraint does not appear in the standard
f(T)

FLRW
Noether equations.

Next,
TEGR
in the presence of a scalar-electromagnetic field coupling is considered
[
1158
]

\mathcal{L}=-\frac{T}{2\kappa^{2}}-\frac{1}{2}\phi_{,\mu}\phi^{,\mu}+V(\phi)+\frac{1}{4}f^{2}(\phi)F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu}\,.

(E.52)

As discussed in Sec. 6.5.2.1, due to the action’s equivalence with its curvature analogue, the same Noether symmetries are expected. An locally rotationally symmetric BT-I model
(b=c)
with
a=b^{m}
for some constant
m
was then considered where the Noether condition constrains the potential and gauge kinetic functions to take the following forms:

V(\phi)\propto\left(c_{1}e^{\mu\phi}-c_{2}e^{-\mu\phi}\right)^{2}\,,\quad f(\phi)\propto\left(c_{1}e^{\mu\phi}-c_{2}e^{-\mu\phi}\right)^{n}\,,

(E.53)

where
\mu=\frac{m+2}{2\sqrt{4m+2}}
and
n=\{\frac{2-m}{2+m},\frac{m}{2+m}\}
is a parameter which value depends on the choice of the electromagnetic vector potential. While a general cosmological behavior was not explored, four special cases were examined in detail: (i)
c_{1}\neq 0,c_{2}=0
, (ii)
c_{1}=0,\,c_{2}\neq 0
and (iii)
c_{1}=c_{2}=1/2
(iv)
c_{1}=-c_{2}=\frac{1}{2}
. With appropriate fine-tuning of parameters, the resulting cosmology can match with observations and also in the last case some interesting potential forms arise that could account for a unified dark matter model.

E.5.4
Cosmological stability and dynamical system approach

In Refs.
[
1148
,
1159
]
, the background cosmological stability of a Kasner universe in the context of
f(T)
gravity was investigated in the case of vacuum. In Ref.
[
1159
]
, a perturbative approach on the background Kasner cosmology was considered, which focuses on perturbing the directional scale factors
\textbf{A}=\{a,b,c\}
via

\textbf{A}=\textbf{A}_{0}\left(1+\varepsilon\textbf{A}_{\varepsilon}\right)+\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{2})\,,

(E.54)

where
\textbf{A}_{0}\propto\left(t^{p_{1}},t^{p_{2}},t^{p_{3}}\right)
is the background Kasner cosmology,
\varepsilon
is an infinitesimal parameter and
\textbf{A}_{\varepsilon}=\left(a_{\varepsilon},b_{\varepsilon},c_{\varepsilon}\right)
represent the directional scale factor perturbations. The stability is determined based on whether
\textbf{A}_{\varepsilon}
grows or decays with time. On the other hand, a numerical integration on the field equations is performed in Ref.
[
1148
]
to investigate the stability of the Kasner cosmology. In both works, the power-law ansatz
f(T)=-T-f_{0}T^{n}
, where
f_{0}
is some constant and
n\in\mathbb{N}
is considered while the exponential model
f(T)=-T-f_{1}\left(1-e^{-pT^{m}}\right)
, where
f_{1},p
and
m
are constants is only considered in Ref.
[
1159
]
.

Starting with the power-law case, as discussed in Sec.
E.5.2
, a Kasner solution only exists when
T=0
or
T^{n-1}=\frac{1}{f_{0}(1-2n)}
. The
T=0
case is an exact solution to the field equations and therefore stability is not considered. For the remaining case, at least for
n\geq 2
, the Kasner solution is unstable and evolves towards a de Sitter attractor, which only exists when
\text{sign}(f_{0})=(-1)^{n}
. While this unstable point is stated to be a saddle point in Ref.
[
1159
]
, it actually represents a source in an expanding universe
[
1148
]
.

For the exponential model case, the Kasner solution is a hyperbolic point (hence cannot be stable) for
m=1
while for
m>1
, the behavior is identical to the power-law case discussed previously. However, the existence of de Sitter attractors it not explored for this case.

Meanwhile, the dynamical behavior of a BT-I cosmology has been investigated in Refs.
[
1159
,
1160
,
1161
]
for the
f(T)=-T-f_{0}T^{n}
ansatz. Starting with Ref.
[
1159
]
in the absence of matter fluids, for
n=2
, the critical points
({H_{a}}^{\star},{H_{b}}^{\star},{H_{c}}^{\star})

P_{\pm}=\pm\left(\frac{1}{6\sqrt{f_{0}}},\frac{1}{6\sqrt{f_{0}}},\frac{1}{6\sqrt{f_{0}}}\right)\,,\quad P_{0}=\left(0,0,0\right)\,,

(E.55)

are obtained.
P_{\pm}
correspond to a
FLRW
de Sitter cosmology while
P_{0}
represents a static universe. Furthermore,
P_{-}
is unstable,
P_{0}
is a saddle point and
P_{+}
is stable, meaning that a BT-I cosmology can isotropize towards a de Sitter late-time behavior. While the full critical point analysis has not been explored for arbitrary
n
, a de Sitter attractor solution only exists when
\text{sign}(f_{0})=(-1)^{n}
.

In Ref.
[
1160
]
, the effect of matter fluids is also considered. The chosen dimensionless phase-space variables are obtained by dividing Eq. (
E.24a
) with
9H^{2}f_{T}
to yield

\tilde{x}:=\frac{T}{9H^{2}}\,,\quad\tilde{y}:=\frac{f_{0}(1-2n)T^{n-1}-1}{f_{T}}\,,\quad\tilde{r}:=\frac{\kappa^{2}\rho}{9H^{2}f_{T}}\,.

(E.56)

As the dynamical variable
\tilde{r}
appears in the Friedmann equations, it can be used to further constrain the parameter space leaving
(\tilde{x},\tilde{y})
as the free dynamical variables. This gives rise to a number of critical points, summarized in Table
38
, which can be associated to distinct cosmological behaviors.

For the special cases
n=2,3
, the overall cosmological dynamical behavior has been analyzed in detail where, it has been observed that the behavior changes depending on the signature of
f_{0}
. Starting with the
n=2
case:

1.

f_{0}>0
: The universe starts at an anisotropic non-standard singularity where
T
finite but
\dot{T}
is divergent, which later isotropizes to either the power-law behavior
(P_{3})
or de Sitter
(P_{4})
.

2.

f_{0}<0
: A non-standard singularity where
T
approaches a point where
f_{T}=0
is identified. The following scenarios are obtained:

(a)

Universe begins at either one of the critical points
P_{1,2,5}
which later evolves to the
P_{3}
behavior;

(b)

The Universe starts and finishes with the aforementioned non-standard singularity, which evolution causes either a cosmological bounce or turnaround;

(c)

Starts at the critical point
P_{1}
which later evolves to the non-standard singularity.

For the
n=3
case,
f_{0}>0
only leads to the behavior described in 2(a) while the remaining cases are all possible for
f_{0}<0
. Therefore, it is possible to realize a late-time accelerating behavior for appropriate parameter choices.

E.5.5
Perspective on anisotropic cosmologies in teleparallel cosmology

Within
TG
, realization of various cosmological behaviors with possible late-time isotropization has been observed. However, further investigations still need to be performed especially since the main attention has been on the background cosmological behavior. Resolving the
H_{0}
tension problem is extremely important for any future model of cosmology, however, an anisotropic cosmology has not yet been shown to be a realistic path in producing the necessary dynamics for this since it would lead to multiple expansion profiles in the different orientations. Meanwhile, only one
TG
extension, that of
f(T)
gravity, has been explored for anisotropic cosmology
40
40

40

While work on
f(T,T_{G})
gravity has been carried out in Ref.
[
1162
]
, for
f(T,T_{G})\propto T_{G}
, the listed field equations still give rise to cosmological dynamics despite the fact that the Lagrangian is expressed in terms of a linear boundary term.
. Additionally, due to the spin connection choice, only the BT-I anisotropic cosmology has been extensively explored. In light of the newly presented good tetrad-spin connection pairs (at least for the
f(T,B)
class), the remaining BT cosmologies may now be explored. All in all, a substantial amount of research still remains to be explored for anisotropic cosmologies.

Appendix F
Cosmological Perturbations in flat FLRW Teleparallel Gravity

This section is devoted in presenting the most important quantities needed for the cosmological perturbations.

F.1
Background

The non-zero components of the torsion tensor and superpotential, and the torsion and boundary term in the background (flat
FLRW
) are

\displaystyle T^{i}{}_{0j}

\displaystyle=H\delta^{i}{}_{j}\,,

(F.1a)

\displaystyle S_{i}{}^{0j}

\displaystyle=-H\delta^{i}{}_{j}\,,

(F.1b)

\displaystyle T

\displaystyle=-6H^{2}\,,

(F.1c)

\displaystyle B

\displaystyle=-6(3H^{2}+\dot{H})\,.

(F.1d)

The matter content is fully conserved giving the standard conservation equation for a perfect fluid

\accentset{\circ}{\nabla}_{\nu}\Theta_{\mu}{}^{\nu}:\,\dot{\rho}+3(\rho+P)=0\,.

(F.2)

F.2
Tensor perturbations

The non-zero components of the torsion tensor and the superpotential are

\displaystyle\delta T^{i}{}_{0j}

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\dot{h}_{ij}\,,

(F.3a)

\displaystyle\delta T^{i}{}_{jk}

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}(\partial_{j}h_{ik}-\partial_{k}h_{ij})\,,

(F.3b)

\displaystyle\delta S_{0}{}^{0i}

\displaystyle=0\,,

(F.3c)

\displaystyle\delta S_{i}{}^{0j}

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{4}\dot{h}_{ij}\,,

(F.3d)

\displaystyle\delta S_{i}{}^{jk}

\displaystyle=-\frac{1}{4a^{2}}(\partial_{j}h_{ik}-\partial_{k}h_{ij})\,,

(F.3e)

while the scalars are

\delta T=0\,,\quad\delta B=0\,.

(F.4)

F.3
Vector and pseudo-vector perturbations

The non-zero components of the vectorial and pseudo-vectorial perturbations for the torsion tensor and the superpotential are

\displaystyle\delta T^{0}{}_{0i}

\displaystyle=\>

\displaystyle a\dot{\beta}_{i}\,,

(F.5a)

\displaystyle\delta T^{i}{}_{0j}

\displaystyle=\>

\displaystyle 2\partial_{i}\dot{h}_{j}-\frac{1}{a}\partial_{j}b_{i}-\epsilon_{kij}\dot{\sigma}_{k}\,,

(F.5b)

\displaystyle\delta T^{0}{}_{ij}

\displaystyle=\>

\displaystyle a(\partial_{i}\beta_{j}-\partial_{j}\beta_{i})\,,

(F.5c)

\displaystyle\delta T^{i}{}_{jk}

\displaystyle=\>

\displaystyle 2(\partial_{i}\partial_{j}h_{k}-\partial_{i}\partial_{k}h_{j})+\epsilon_{ijl}\partial_{k}\sigma_{l}-\epsilon_{ikl}\partial_{j}\sigma_{l}\,,

(F.5d)

\displaystyle\delta S_{0}{}^{0i}

\displaystyle=\>

\displaystyle-\frac{1}{2a^{2}}\Big[2aH(b_{i}-\beta_{i})+\epsilon_{ilk}\partial_{k}\sigma_{l}\Big]\,,

(F.5e)

\displaystyle\delta S_{i}{}^{0j}

\displaystyle=\>

\displaystyle-\frac{1}{2a}\Big[\frac{1}{2}\Big(\partial_{i}(b_{j}+\beta_{j}-a\dot{h}_{j})+\partial_{j}(b_{i}-\beta_{i}-a\dot{h}_{i})\Big)\Big]\,,

(F.5f)

\displaystyle\delta S_{0}{}^{ij}

\displaystyle=\>

\displaystyle-\frac{1}{4a^{3}}\Big[\partial_{i}(b_{j}-\beta_{j}+2a\dot{h}_{j})-\partial_{j}(b_{i}-\beta_{i}+2a\dot{h}_{i})-2a\epsilon_{lij}\dot{\sigma}_{l}\Big]\,,

(F.5g)

\displaystyle\delta S_{i}{}^{jk}

\displaystyle=\>

\displaystyle-\frac{1}{2a^{2}}\Big[\delta_{im}\epsilon_{kjl}\partial_{l}\sigma_{m}+\delta_{ij}\Big(2aH(b_{k}-\beta_{k})-a\dot{\beta}_{k}-2\partial^{2}h_{k}\Big)

\displaystyle-\delta_{ik}\Big(2aH(b_{j}-\beta_{j})-a\dot{\beta}_{j}-2\partial^{2}h_{j}\Big)-2\delta_{il}\partial_{k}\partial_{l}h_{j}+2\delta_{kl}\partial_{i}\partial_{j}h_{l}\Big]\,,

(F.5h)

and the perturbations related to the torsion and boundary term scalars are

\delta T=0\,,\quad\delta B=0\,.

(F.6)

F.4
Scalar and pseudo-scalar perturbations

The components of the torsion tensor and the superpotential for scalar and pseudo-scalar perturbations up to first order are

\displaystyle\delta T^{0}{}_{0i}

\displaystyle=\partial_{i}(a\dot{\beta}-\phi)\,,

(F.7a)

\displaystyle\delta T^{i}{}_{0j}

\displaystyle=\partial_{i}\partial_{j}(\dot{h}-a^{-1}b)-\epsilon_{lij}\partial_{l}\dot{\sigma}-\dot{\psi}\delta_{ij}\,,

(F.7b)

\displaystyle\delta T^{0}{}_{ij}

\displaystyle=0\,,

(F.7c)

\displaystyle\delta T^{i}{}_{jk}

\displaystyle=\delta_{ij}\partial_{k}\psi-\delta_{ik}\partial_{j}\psi+\delta_{il}(\epsilon_{klm}\partial_{j}\partial_{m}\sigma-\epsilon_{jlm}\partial_{k}\partial_{m}\sigma)\,,

(F.7d)

\displaystyle\delta S_{0}{}^{0i}

\displaystyle=-\frac{H}{a}\partial_{i}\Big(b-\beta-(aH)^{-1}\psi\Big)\,,

(F.7e)

\displaystyle\delta S_{i}{}^{0j}

\displaystyle=\Big[(2H\phi+\dot{\psi})\delta_{ij}+\frac{1}{2}\partial_{i}\partial_{j}(\dot{h}-a^{-1}b)-\frac{1}{2}\partial^{2}(\dot{h}-a^{-1}b)\delta_{ij}\Big]\,,

(F.7f)

\displaystyle\delta S_{0}{}^{ij}

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2a^{2}}\epsilon_{ijk}\partial_{k}\dot{\sigma}\,,

(F.7g)

\displaystyle\delta S_{i}{}^{jk}

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2a^{2}}\Big[\delta_{ik}\partial_{j}\Big(2aH(b-\beta)+\phi-\psi-a\dot{\beta}\Big)-\delta_{ij}\partial_{k}\Big(2aH(b-\beta)+\phi-\psi-a\dot{\beta}\Big)\Big]\,,

(F.7h)

and the perturbations up to first order to the scalar torsion and boundary term become

\displaystyle\delta T

\displaystyle=\>

\displaystyle 4H\Big(3H\phi+3\dot{\psi}+\frac{1}{a}\partial^{2}b-\partial^{2}\dot{h}\Big)\,,

(F.8a)

\displaystyle\delta B

\displaystyle=\>

\displaystyle-\Big[H\left(\frac{1}{a}\partial^{2}(6\beta-10b)-6(6\dot{\psi}+\dot{\phi}-2\partial^{2}\dot{h}+6H\phi)\right)+\frac{2}{a}\partial^{2}(\dot{\beta}-\dot{b})+\frac{2}{a^{2}}\partial^{2}(2\psi-\phi)

\displaystyle+2(\partial^{2}\ddot{h}-6\dot{H}\phi-3\ddot{\psi})\Big]\,.

(F.8b)

Then, the perturbation conservation equations become

\displaystyle\accentset{\circ}{\nabla}_{\mu}\Theta_{0}{}^{\mu}

\displaystyle=\delta\dot{\rho}+3H(\delta p+\delta\rho)+\frac{\partial^{2}v(p+\rho)}{a}-3\dot{\psi}(p+\rho)+\partial^{2}\dot{h}(p+\rho)=0\,,

(F.9a)

\displaystyle\accentset{\circ}{\nabla}_{\mu}\Theta_{i}{}^{\mu}

\displaystyle=\partial_{i}\Big[\delta p+(\rho+p)\Big(4aH(b+v-\beta)+\phi+a(\dot{b}-\dot{\beta}+\dot{v})\Big)+a(\dot{\rho}+\dot{p})(v+b-\beta)\Big]=0\,.

(F.9b)

F.5
Sub-horizon limit in the Newtonian gauge

The torsion scalar, the boundary term and the arbitrary functions of them, become in the Newtonian gauge

\displaystyle\delta T

\displaystyle\simeq-\frac{4H}{a}\left(k^{2}b-3aH(\psi+\phi)\right)\,,

(F.10a)

\displaystyle\delta B

\displaystyle\simeq-\frac{2k^{2}}{a^{2}}(2abH-2\psi+\phi)\,,

(F.10b)

\displaystyle\delta f_{T}

\displaystyle\simeq-\frac{2k^{2}}{a^{2}}\left(2abH\left(f_{TB}+f_{TT}\right)+f_{TB}(\phi-2\psi)\right)\,,

(F.10c)

\displaystyle\delta f_{B}

\displaystyle\simeq-\frac{2k^{2}}{a^{2}}\left(2abH(f_{BB}+f_{TB})+f_{BB}(\phi-2\psi)\right)\,.

(F.10d)

Appendix G
Boltzmann equations analysis

At the present time, the
CMB
dominates the constraints on the standard model of cosmology. This era of precision cosmology can be seen through plots of the current status of the power spectra coming from the
CMB
. Furthermore, this spectrum carries relevant information on both the early- and late-time Universe. We can take advantage of modified versions of the
CLASS
code
41
41

41

Another example of numerical code is
hiCLASS
, which can compute predictions for modified models in Horndeski gravity. However, our new code can consider any
additional
modification as an effective fluid derived from the numerical solution of the field equation in a generic way.
to analyze the perturbations. This implementation allows the analysis of structure formation since each power spectrum is related to the curvature, baryonic matter, dark matter, etc. We start with the perturbations obtained for
\Lambda
CDM
and afterwards we carry out a modified version that includes any modified/extended theory as an effective-like fluid. The effects will be seen as deviations in the power spectrum. These perturbations are described by equations for density contrast and velocity divergence in the synchronous gauge and valid for a perfect fluid (see Sec. 7 for examples on the procedure through which these perturbations are implemented)
[
1163
,
1164
]

\displaystyle\dot{\delta}_{i}+3\mathcal{H}(c^{2}_{s,\rm eff}-w_{i})\left[\delta_{i}+3\mathcal{H}(1+w_{i})\frac{v_{i}}{k}\right]+(1+\omega_{i})kv_{i}+3\mathcal{H}\dot{w}_{i}\frac{v_{i}}{k}

\displaystyle=-3(1+w_{i})\dot{h}\,,

(G.1a)

\displaystyle\dot{v}_{i}+\mathcal{H}(1-3c^{2}_{s,\rm eff})v_{i}

\displaystyle=\frac{k\delta_{i}c^{2}_{s,\rm eff}}{1+w_{i}}\,.

(G.1b)

The derivatives denoted by dots are
wrt
the conformal time,
\mathcal{H}
is the conformal Hubble parameter,
c^{2}_{s,\rm eff}
is the effective sound speed,
v_{i}
is the velocity of the
i
th fluid,
\delta_{i}
are the perturbations of each matter component, i.e baryons, photons, radiation, cold dark matter, and
w_{i}
is the
EoS
for each component and
k
is the wave mode. One way to implement these equations of motion is through the Parameterized Post-Friedmann
[
1165
]
approach in the
CLASS
code, which is written in the programming language C and requires no specific version of the compiler; it has flexibility because it is not hard coded, it has a clear structure and a dynamical allocation of all indices. Furthermore, it controls accuracy as all accuracy parameters are grouped within a single structure; and finally it is faster than other codes.

In order to work with
CLASS
, one has to express quantities and equations in terms of the specific code units. The units for the wavenumbers
k
and the Hubble parameter in the conformal time
\mathcal{H}
are 1/Mpc, while the conformal time
\tau
has the units of Mpc. Also, we employ the units from Sec. 1.3. Finally, the default
CMB
multipoles (
C_{l}
’s) are dimensionless. A schematic architecture is depicted in Fig.
51
and the process to implement
TG
models is illustrated (with their equations) in the top left panels of Figs.
52
–
53
.

G.1
A note on Boltzmann equations at numerical code level

From Eq. (
G.1b
), we can rewrite the full perturbed system of equations that includes the full Boltzmann equations: photons, neutrinos, baryons,
CDM
, plus the perturbed Einstein equations in Sec. 7.7.2 as

\displaystyle\frac{d\Theta_{0}}{d\eta}+k\Theta_{1}

\displaystyle=-\frac{d\Phi}{d\eta}\,,

(G.2a)

\displaystyle\frac{d\Theta_{1}}{d\eta}-\frac{k}{3}\Theta_{0}

\displaystyle=-\frac{k}{3}\Phi

(G.2b)

\displaystyle\frac{d\delta}{d\eta}+ikv

\displaystyle=-3\frac{d\Phi}{d\eta}\,,

(G.2c)

\displaystyle\frac{dv}{d\eta}+\frac{1}{a}\frac{da}{d\eta}

\displaystyle=ik\Phi\,,

(G.2d)

\displaystyle k^{2}\Phi+3\frac{1}{a}\frac{da}{d\eta}\left(\frac{d\Phi}{d\eta}+\frac{1}{a}\frac{da}{d\eta}\Phi\right)

\displaystyle=4\pi Ga^{2}\left[\rho_{m}\delta+4\rho_{r}\Theta_{0}\right]\,,

(G.2e)

where the time variable is the conformal time (
d\eta=dt/a
, where
a
is the scale factor) and
k
is the comoving wavenumber. The primary components of the photon distribution that affect the matter variables are the monopole and dipole moments denoted by
\Theta_{0}
and
\Theta_{1}
respectively. The matter fluctuations are characterized by the overdensity
\delta
and the irrotational peculiar velocity
v
. Or by each component (and for numerical code purposes):

\displaystyle\dot{\delta}

\displaystyle=-ku-3\dot{\Phi}\,,

(G.3a)

\displaystyle\dot{u}

\displaystyle=-\frac{\dot{a}}{a}u+k\Psi\,,

(G.3b)

\displaystyle\dot{\delta_{b}}

\displaystyle=-ku_{b}-3\dot{\Phi}\,,

(G.3c)

\displaystyle\dot{u_{b}}

\displaystyle=-\frac{\dot{a}}{a}u_{b}+k\Psi+kc_{s}^{2}\delta_{b}+\frac{\dot{\tau}}{R}[u_{b}-3\Theta_{1}]\,,

(G.3d)

\displaystyle\dot{\Theta}_{0}

\displaystyle=-k\Theta_{1}-\dot{\Phi}\,,

(G.3e)

\displaystyle\dot{\Theta}_{1}

\displaystyle=\frac{k}{3}\left[\Theta_{0}-2\Theta_{2}+\Psi\right]+\dot{\tau}\left[\Theta_{1}-\frac{u_{b}}{3}\right]\,,

(G.3f)

\displaystyle\dot{\Theta}_{2}

\displaystyle=\frac{k}{5}\left[2\Theta_{1}-3\Theta_{3}\right]+\dot{\tau}\left[\Theta_{2}-\frac{\Pi}{10}\right]\,,

(G.3g)

\displaystyle\dot{\Theta}_{l}

\displaystyle=\frac{k}{2l+1}\left[l\Theta_{l-1}-(l+1)\Theta_{l+1}\right]+\dot{\tau}\Theta_{l}\,,\quad l>2\,,

(G.3h)

\displaystyle\dot{\Theta}_{Pl}

\displaystyle=\frac{k}{2l+1}\left[l\Theta_{P(l-1)}-(l+1)\Theta_{P(l+1)}\right]+\dot{\tau}\left[\Theta_{Pl}-\frac{\Pi}{2}(\delta_{l,0}+\frac{\delta_{l,2}}{5})\right]\,,

(G.3i)

\displaystyle\dot{\mathcal{N}}_{0}

\displaystyle=-k\mathcal{N}_{1}-\dot{\Phi}\,,

(G.3j)

\displaystyle\dot{\mathcal{N}}_{1}

\displaystyle=\frac{k}{3}\left[\mathcal{N}_{0}-2\mathcal{N}_{2}+\Psi\right]\,,

(G.3k)

\displaystyle\dot{\mathcal{N}}_{l}

\displaystyle=\frac{k}{2l+1}\left[l\mathcal{N}_{l-1}-(l+1)\mathcal{N}_{l+1}\right]\,,\quad l>1\,,

(G.3l)

\displaystyle k^{2}\Phi+3\frac{\dot{a}}{a}\left(\dot{\Phi}-\frac{\dot{a}}{a}\Psi\right)

\displaystyle=4\pi Ga^{2}\left[\rho_{m}\delta_{m}+4\rho_{r}\Theta_{r0}\right]\,,

(G.3m)

where dot denotes derivatives
wrt
conformal time
\eta
,
\delta
(
\delta_{b}
) and
u
(
u_{b}
) are the density and velocity perturbations for the dark matter (baryons),
\Theta_{l}
and
\Theta_{Pl}
are the photon temperature and polarization multipole moments,
{\mathcal{N}}_{l}
are the multipole moments of the (massless) neutrino temperature, and
\Pi=\Theta_{2}+\Theta_{P0}+\Theta_{P2}
. The baryon-to-photon ratio is given by
R=3\rho_{b}/(4\rho_{\gamma})
,
\tau
is the Thomson scattering optical depth and
c_{s}
is the baryon sound speed. The subscripts

and

\rho_{r}
and
\rho_{m}

Appendix H
Surveys and cosmological data

The interest in understanding the physics of the late Universe can be well comprehended by using observational data from:
SN
eIa luminosity distances from the Pantheon compilation
[
871
]
,
BAO
from redshift surveys
[

,
1167
,

]

[

To carry out cosmological tests on the free parameters that can be considered in the

\Omega_{\rm m0}
and

[

The survey compilations considered for these studies described in this Review are provided in the following sections.

H.1
Galaxy ages compilations

Modified gravity constraints have been studied through measurements related to the galaxy ages. Currently, this kind of observable includes a sample of 51 observations in the redshift range
0.07<z<2.0

[
801
]
. A calibration using stellar evolution from the BC03 model
[
1171
]
of this sample was presented in Ref.
[

]
reducing this sample to 31 data points. The normalized parameter
h(z)
can be computed by considering the values from

+
